passage: Beatriz had been baking custard tarts in her Porto kitchen since five, humming. Her weekend market stall opened in two weeks, and she believed in it completely. Still, on the fridge hung a list her friend Lindiwe had teased her about: "Three months of rent put aside. Two cafés who'd take wholesale orders. Stall date plus two weeks, just in case." On Tuesday the council emailed: the market would close for a month for repairs. Lindiwe came round expecting tears. Instead Beatriz was on the phone to the first café. "It's a delay, not a verdict," she said, sliding a tray into the oven. "The tarts are still good. I'm still good. The plan just moves." By evening, one café had ordered forty tarts for Saturday.

qa.q: Why was the market closing?
qa.a: The market would close for a month for repairs.

qa.q: What does 'It's a delay, not a verdict' show about how Beatriz sees the setback?
qa.a: It shows the closure hit her plan, not her belief in herself or her tarts, so she can stay hopeful and act. 🙂

qa.q: Which part of Beatriz's preparation helped most, and why?
qa.a: The café idea on the fridge list helped most, because it gave her a ready second route she could call the same day.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe's view of the list change?
qa.a: Lindiwe teased her about the list and came expecting tears, but then watched it turn a closure into a Saturday order.

grounding: A hopeful young baker keeps savings, backup buyers and a time buffer, so a market closure hits her plan but not her sense of self.

passage: In the NGO's cramped office above a pharmacy, Meenal pinned her plan for the children's reading festival on the wall. Siddharth read it and raised an eyebrow. "You've got a whole column called 'If this fails'." "I expect it to go brilliantly," Meenal said. "That's why I'll work nights on it. But the school hall is booked for a backup date, a tenth of the budget is kept for surprises, and the storyteller has a stand-in." Three weeks later, the main sponsor cut its money by half, two days before the event. Pradeep, the director, came in looking grim. Meenal had already opened her 'If this fails' column. The surprise money covered the printing, and the book stall moved into the free school hall. "Annoying," she said, crossing out a line. "But it's the plan that took the hit. Not me."

qa.q: What was the column on Meenal's plan called?
qa.a: The column was called 'If this fails'.

qa.q: How can you tell Meenal is still hopeful about the festival?
qa.a: She says she expects it to go brilliantly and will work nights on it, so the backup column is preparation, not doubt.

qa.q: What could other planners borrow from Meenal's approach?
qa.a: Keep a backup date or venue, set aside part of the budget for surprises, and decide the fallback before trouble starts.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when he sees Meenal already handling it?
qa.a: Pradeep came in grim, so Pradeep would likely feel relief and more trust in Meenal's planning.

grounding: An NGO planner stays hopeful but builds a backup date, a surprise fund and a fallback, so a sponsor cut hits the plan and not her.

passage:
Dear Lalit,
You asked how I stay so calm about the film course in Chennai. Honestly, I'm excited. I think I'll get in, and I'm working like I will: portfolio done, two short films shot.
But here's what I didn't tell you. I've applied to two other courses too, one online. I've kept four months of expenses in a separate account I don't touch. And I told Santosh sir at the studio I could keep editing part-time if the course is delayed.
Yesterday it was. The institute moved admissions to next year.
I cried for about ten minutes. Then I opened my list and called Santosh sir. I start part-time on Monday, and my portfolio gets one more year to grow.
The course said "not yet". It didn't say "not you".
Your big sister,
Kaveri

qa.q: What did the institute do yesterday?
qa.a: The institute moved admissions to next year.

qa.q: What does 'It didn't say not you' show about Kaveri's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Kaveri was sad but saw the delay as a setback to her plan, not a judgement on her worth.

qa.q: What made Kaveri's quick recovery possible?
qa.a: Her backups were ready before the news: two other applications, four months of expenses set aside, and part-time editing with Santosh sir.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Kaveri's calm after this letter?
qa.a: Lalit might realise her calm comes from quiet preparation, not luck, and feel proud of her. 🤍

grounding: A young woman stays hopeful about a film course while keeping other applications, savings and part-time work ready, so a delay doesn't shake her.

passage:
Hrithik, you asked how I stayed calm when the bakery contract fell through. I'm Rukhsar, and I'll tell you honestly, I'm still an optimist. My Ammi calls me her stubborn girl.
When I left my job to start supplying cakes to cafés in Lucknow, I believed in it completely. I worked like it was going to succeed: tasting every recipe, visiting every café owner myself.
But I also made myself sit down with a notebook and write: what if the biggest café drops me? I kept three months of expenses aside and didn't touch it. I kept my old manager's number and told her I might ask for freelance work. And I built a buffer into every delivery date.
In March, the biggest café did drop me. It stung for a day. But nothing collapsed. I used the buffer, took two freelance projects, and found two new cafés by May. The plan got bruised, not me.

qa.q: What happened in March?
qa.a: In March, the biggest café did drop Rukhsar.

qa.q: Why did losing the café only sting for a day, instead of shaking Rukhsar's confidence?
qa.a: She had already imagined it and prepared, so the setback felt like a problem for the plan, not proof that she was a failure.

qa.q: Which choices, made in advance, protected Rukhsar when the contract fell through?
qa.a: She kept three months of expenses aside, kept her old manager's number for freelance work and built a buffer into every delivery date.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Rukhsar's approach after hearing this?
qa.a: Hrithik may realise that being an optimist and planning for setbacks can go together, since Rukhsar worked as if she'd succeed and still had a plan B.

grounding: It shows a planner keeping her optimism for effort while adding a buffer, savings and a plan B, so a setback hurts the plan rather than her sense of self.

passage:
I'm Salma, and I've lived next door to Elizabeth in our building in Nairobi for two years. Last spring she quit her office job to open a small pottery studio in the garage. She was so sure of it, glowing, telling everyone about the classes she'd teach.
What I noticed, though, was that she kept doing her old accounting work two evenings a week. When I asked why, she laughed. "Because I believe in the studio, and I also like eating."
In June the kiln cracked and the studio closed for a month. I expected her to fall apart. She was upset, yes, I saw her sitting on the steps. But the next morning she was on the phone about repairs, and she took on a few more accounting evenings.
I can't say what she felt inside. From outside, it looked like the setback hit her plan, not her.

qa.q: What cracked in June?
qa.a: The kiln cracked.

qa.q: What do Elizabeth's words 'I believe in the studio, and I also like eating' suggest about how she thought?
qa.a: They suggest she was truly hopeful about the studio but also realistic, wanting a steady backup so her hope wouldn't leave her stuck.

qa.q: What choice made the kiln breaking easier for Elizabeth to handle?
qa.a: Keeping her accounting work two evenings a week, and adding a few more when the studio closed, meant the setback didn't leave her with nothing.

qa.q: How did Salma's expectations differ from what actually happened?
qa.a: Salma expected Elizabeth to fall apart when the kiln cracked, but saw her upset for a while and then calmly making calls the next morning.

grounding: Told by a neighbour, it shows a planner who keeps optimism for effort while holding a plan B, so a setback hits her plan rather than her sense of self.
